```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 5
)

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))
options(scipen = 999)
```

# 1. Load the MoMA datasets

This demonstration uses MoMA's open `Artworks.csv` and `Artists.csv` files.

Dataset source: https://github.com/MuseumofModernArt/collection

```{r load-data}
artwork_files <- c("Artworks.csv", "Artworks(1).csv")
artist_files <- c("Artists.csv", "Artists(1).csv")

artwork_file <- artwork_files[file.exists(artwork_files)][1]
artist_file <- artist_files[file.exists(artist_files)][1]

if (is.na(artwork_file) || is.na(artist_file)) {
  stop("Put Artworks.csv and Artists.csv in the same folder as this RMD file.")
}

artworks <- read_csv(artwork_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
artists <- read_csv(artist_file, show_col_types = FALSE)

tibble(
  Dataset = c("Artworks", "Artists"),
  Rows = c(nrow(artworks), nrow(artists)),
  Columns = c(ncol(artworks), ncol(artists))
) %>%
  kable(caption = "Dataset size")
```

# 2. Completeness check

I start with four fields that are important for finding and understanding an artwork: artist, date, medium and dimensions.

```{r completeness}
core_missing <- tibble(
  Field = c("Artist", "Date", "Medium", "Dimensions"),
  Missing = c(
    sum(is.na(artworks$Artist)),
    sum(is.na(artworks$Date)),
    sum(is.na(artworks$Medium)),
    sum(is.na(artworks$Dimensions))
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    Percent = 100 * Missing / nrow(artworks)
  )

core_missing %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Missing values in core artwork fields")

ggplot(core_missing, aes(x = reorder(Field, Missing), y = Missing)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Missing values in four core artwork fields",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of records"
  )
```

# 3. Build four transparent screening signals

The demonstration uses four simple signals:

1. at least one missing core field;
2. extra leading or trailing whitespace in `Medium`;
3. a chronological contradiction where a simple artwork year is earlier than the creator's recorded `BeginDate`;
4. an unusually large height or width above the 99.9th percentile.

These are screening signals, not automatic proof that a museum record is wrong.

```{r build-signals}
artists_small <- artists %>%
  transmute(
    ArtistID = ConstituentID,
    CreatorBegin = BeginDate,
    CreatorEnd = EndDate
  )

analysis <- artworks %>%
  mutate(
    Missing_Key_Count =
      is.na(Artist) +
      is.na(Date) +
      is.na(Medium) +
      is.na(Dimensions),

    Missing_Flag = Missing_Key_Count > 0,

    Medium_Format_Flag =
      !is.na(Medium) & Medium != str_trim(Medium),

    Single_Artist = replace_na(
      str_detect(as.character(ConstituentID), "^\\d+$"),
      FALSE
    ),

    ArtistID = if_else(
      Single_Artist,
      as.integer(ConstituentID),
      NA_integer_
    ),

    Date_Clean = str_trim(replace_na(Date, "")),

    Simple_Date = str_detect(
      Date_Clean,
      regex("^(?:c\\.\\s*)?\\(?\\d{4}\\)?$", ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),

    Work_Year = as.integer(str_extract(Date_Clean, "\\d{4}"))
  ) %>%
  left_join(artists_small, by = "ArtistID")

height_cutoff <- quantile(
  analysis$`Height (cm)`[analysis$`Height (cm)` > 0],
  0.999,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

width_cutoff <- quantile(
  analysis$`Width (cm)`[analysis$`Width (cm)` > 0],
  0.999,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

analysis <- analysis %>%
  mutate(
    Logical_Date_Flag = replace_na(
      Single_Artist &
        Simple_Date &
        !is.na(CreatorBegin) &
        CreatorBegin > 0 &
        Work_Year < CreatorBegin,
      FALSE
    ),

    Extreme_Size_Flag = replace_na(
      (`Height (cm)` > height_cutoff) |
        (`Width (cm)` > width_cutoff),
      FALSE
    ),

    Signal_Count =
      as.integer(Missing_Flag) +
      as.integer(Medium_Format_Flag) +
      as.integer(Logical_Date_Flag) +
      as.integer(Extreme_Size_Flag),

    Priority_Tier = case_when(
      Logical_Date_Flag ~ "Tier 1 - logical contradiction",
      Signal_Count >= 2 ~ "Tier 2 - multiple signals",
      Signal_Count == 1 ~ "Tier 3 - single signal",
      TRUE ~ "No flag"
    )
  )
```

# 4. What did the screening find?

```{r signal-summary}
signal_summary <- tibble(
  Signal = c(
    "Missing core field(s)",
    "Medium formatting",
    "Logical date contradiction",
    "Extreme size"
  ),
  Records = c(
    sum(analysis$Missing_Flag, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(analysis$Medium_Format_Flag, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(analysis$Logical_Date_Flag, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(analysis$Extreme_Size_Flag, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
)

signal_summary %>%
  kable(caption = "Number of records flagged by each signal")

ggplot(signal_summary, aes(x = reorder(Signal, Records), y = Records)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Records flagged by each screening signal",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of records"
  )
```

The `Medium` field also contains formatting variants that disappear after trimming whitespace.

```{r medium-standardisation}
medium_summary <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Unique Medium values before trimming",
    "Unique Medium values after trimming",
    "Records with leading/trailing whitespace"
  ),
  Value = c(
    n_distinct(artworks$Medium, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_distinct(str_trim(artworks$Medium), na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(analysis$Medium_Format_Flag, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
)

medium_summary %>%
  kable(caption = "Medium standardisation check")
```

# 5. Review-priority tiers

Logical contradictions receive the highest tier. Records with two or more independent signals are next, followed by records with one signal.

```{r priority-tiers}
priority_summary <- analysis %>%
  count(Priority_Tier) %>%
  mutate(
    Percent = 100 * n / nrow(analysis)
  )

priority_summary %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Review-priority tiers")

priority_plot <- priority_summary %>%
  mutate(
    Priority_Tier = factor(
      Priority_Tier,
      levels = c(
        "No flag",
        "Tier 3 - single signal",
        "Tier 2 - multiple signals",
        "Tier 1 - logical contradiction"
      )
    )
  )

ggplot(priority_plot, aes(x = Priority_Tier, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Review-priority tiers",
    subtitle = "Log scale is used because the groups differ greatly in size",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of records (log scale)"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))
```

The most useful first-pass queue is Tier 1 plus Tier 2.

```{r review-reduction}
high_priority_n <- sum(
  analysis$Priority_Tier %in%
    c("Tier 1 - logical contradiction", "Tier 2 - multiple signals")
)

tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Total artwork records",
    "Tier 1 + Tier 2 records",
    "Share of collection (%)",
    "Approximate reduction factor"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(analysis),
    high_priority_n,
    100 * high_priority_n / nrow(analysis),
    nrow(analysis) / high_priority_n
  )
) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "First-pass review workload")
```

This shows whether the method can reduce a very large catalogue to a much smaller group for expert review.

# 6. Strong chronological flags

To reduce false positives, this rule is deliberately conservative. It only uses single-creator records and simple date expressions such as `1903`, `(1995)` or `c. 1940`.

`BeginDate` can represent a person's birth year or an organisation's recorded start year, so every result still requires human interpretation.

```{r logical-flags}
logical_cases <- analysis %>%
  filter(Logical_Date_Flag) %>%
  select(
    ObjectID,
    Title,
    Artist,
    Date,
    Work_Year,
    CreatorBegin,
    CreatorEnd,
    Department
  ) %>%
  arrange(Work_Year)

logical_cases %>%
  kable(caption = "Tier 1 chronological review candidates")
```

The known Johan Thorn Prikker example from the proposal should appear in this table.

```{r prikker-check}
analysis %>%
  filter(ObjectID == 6521) %>%
  select(
    ObjectID,
    Title,
    Artist,
    Date,
    Work_Year,
    CreatorBegin,
    CreatorEnd,
    Logical_Date_Flag,
    Priority_Tier
  ) %>%
  kable(caption = "Johan Thorn Prikker feasibility check")
```

# 7. Are flags evenly distributed across departments?

A high flag rate does not automatically mean poor-quality metadata. Different departments describe different kinds of objects, so this check is important for interpretation and fairness.

```{r department-check}
department_summary <- analysis %>%
  mutate(
    Department = replace_na(Department, "Unknown")
  ) %>%
  group_by(Department) %>%
  summarise(
    Records = n(),
    Flagged = sum(Signal_Count > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    Flag_Rate = 100 * Flagged / Records,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(Flag_Rate))

department_summary %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Flag rate by department")

ggplot(
  department_summary,
  aes(x = reorder(Department, Flag_Rate), y = Flag_Rate)
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Share of records with at least one flag by department",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Flagged records (%)"
  )
```

# 8. Example review queue

The queue below is ordered by tier, then by the number of independent signals. It does not automatically correct any museum record.

```{r review-queue}
review_queue <- analysis %>%
  filter(Priority_Tier != "No flag") %>%
  mutate(
    Priority_Order = case_when(
      Priority_Tier == "Tier 1 - logical contradiction" ~ 1,
      Priority_Tier == "Tier 2 - multiple signals" ~ 2,
      TRUE ~ 3
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    Priority_Order,
    desc(Signal_Count),
    desc(Missing_Key_Count)
  ) %>%
  select(
    ObjectID,
    Title,
    Artist,
    Department,
    Date,
    Signal_Count,
    Missing_Key_Count,
    Medium_Format_Flag,
    Logical_Date_Flag,
    Extreme_Size_Flag,
    Priority_Tier
  )

head(review_queue, 20) %>%
  kable(caption = "First 20 records in the review queue")
```

# 9. Demonstration conclusion

This demonstration shows that the project is feasible using ordinary tabular museum data and simple R methods. The four signals create an explainable review-priority system rather than an automatic correction system. The most important result is whether Tier 1 and Tier 2 reduce the full catalogue to a small first-pass review queue while still recovering known examples such as Johan Thorn Prikker.

The department comparison also shows an important limitation: flag rates can reflect different cataloguing practices or object types, so a high flag rate must not automatically be interpreted as poor data quality.
